name: A Burns ranch lot

place_source.title: Wikidata: Burns (Q6178257), coordinate location and elevation above sea level

blurb: A ranch lot on the sagebrush steppe at the edge of the Harney Basin: a windbreak of juniper and pine, open grass and bare ground, a stock pond, and fences and posts where black-billed magpies, western meadowlarks and ravens sit. Ground squirrels work the morning before the heat, mule deer cross at dusk, and a Columbia spotted frog sits at the pond when the nights turn warm.

facts.text: Burns has a semi-arid continental climate (Köppen BSk) bordering on a continental Mediterranean climate (Dsb), with about 99 days of precipitation a year.

source.title: Wikipedia contributors, "Burns, Oregon", English Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0

facts.text: Normal annual precipitation in Burns is about 11 inches (279 mm), including 34 inches (86 cm) of snow, and the growing season between the first and last freezing temperatures is about 72 days.

source.title: Wikipedia contributors, "Burns, Oregon", English Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0

facts.text: About 65 percent of Harney County's 2011 agricultural revenue came from cattle sales and 29 percent from alfalfa hay, and cattle ranching in the region began as early as the 1860s.

facts.text: Harney County is the largest county in Oregon by area and the tenth largest in the United States, covering about 10,000 square miles with a total population of roughly 7,600.

facts.text: The sage thrasher is a sagebrush obligate: it depends on big sagebrush for nesting and is therefore vulnerable to habitat loss, including shrubsteppe converted to urban or agricultural land.

facts.text: Belding's ground squirrels leave their burrows at sunrise, are most active in the morning, and go back under ground at sunset, having spent as much as 40 percent of the summer eating.

facts.text: Black-tailed jackrabbits need shrubs or small conifers for hiding, nesting and thermal cover, and grass for night feeding; they do not habitually use burrows.
